newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist says government mimics Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist says government mimics Le Pen.

text.p: Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin accused the French government on Saturday of dangerously seeking to lure voters from the extreme-right National Front party by mimicking its anti-immigrant ideas.

"The right is not a bulwark against the extreme-right," Jospin told a party meeting discussing ways to combat the Front, a dominant theme among mainstream parties a year before parliamentary elections.
Jospin said parties in Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right coalition were adopting an accommodating attitude towards Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front and following up its ideas.
"The right is scared of the extreme right in the elections. It wants to recapture the extreme right instead of fighting it," he said.

Le Pen, who wants to expel three million immigrants as a way of cutting high unemployment, took 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election won by Jacques Chirac. The Front won a fourth town hall in municipal elections last month in the southern town of Vitrolles.
The government says the Socialists boosted the far-right by a too-liberal policy towards immigration under late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand from 1981-94.

The French parliament is expected to pass a controversial bill by the end of March tightening already strict immigration rules. It will grant police wider powers to monitor immigrants via searches or fingerprinting.

Jospin said a government strategy of lumping together the Socialists and the National Front as threats was "dangerous because it trivialises the extreme right under the pretext of demonising the left."

The party discussed a report containing 15 proposals to defuse the Front, including withdrawing candidates from three-way run-offs in elections if it would strengthen the chances of a mainstream candidate beating a Front member.

A few Socialists, like former party boss Henri Emmanuelli, favour banning the Front after Le Pen last year openly espoused a doctrine of racial inequality. But most Socialists fear a ban would backfire.
"I don't think you lower a fever by breaking the thermometer," said former Socialist culture minister Jack Lang, a strong opponent of a ban.
